name: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)
text:
# Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF)
Also called: Reflectance equation
## Overview
The Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) provides the ratio of flux concentration per steradian reflected into a given direction as a consequence of differential irradiance incident from another given direction [S1, unofficial]. It serves as the core component of the [Surface Rendering Equation](14578-surface-rendering-equation.md), defining the reflected radiance at a surface point [S1, unofficial].
## Shared principles
The BRDF, denoted as $f(\vec{\omega}_i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}_r)$, is defined as the ratio of the reflected radiance $L_r(\vec{\omega}_r)$ to the incident irradiance $E(\vec{\omega}_i)$ [S1, unofficial].

$$f(\vec{\omega}_i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}_r) = \frac{L_r(\vec{\omega}_r)}{E(\vec{\omega}_i)} = \frac{L_r(\vec{\omega}_r)}{L_i(\vec{\omega}_i) \cos \theta d\omega_i}$$

where $\theta$ is the angle between the incident direction $\vec{\omega}_i$ and the surface normal, and $d\omega_i$ is the differential solid angle [S1, unofficial]. The total reflected radiance $L_r(\vec{\omega}_r)$ in a specific outgoing direction $\vec{\omega}_r$ is obtained by integrating the product of the BRDF, the incident radiance, and the cosine term over the hemisphere of incident directions $\Omega_i$ [S1, unofficial]. This integral is known as the reflectance equation:

$$L_r(\vec{\omega}_r) = \int_{\Omega_i} f(\vec{\omega}_i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}_r) L_i(\vec{\omega}_i) \cos \theta d\omega_i$$

For physically plausible materials, the BRDF must satisfy the Helmholtz reciprocity principle, meaning $f(\vec{\omega}_i \rightarrow \vec{\omega}_r) = f(\vec{\omega}_r \rightarrow \vec{\omega}_i)$, and the energy conservation principle, where the total reflected energy does not exceed the incident energy [G].
## Subtopics

### Microfacet BRDF
Models surfaces as a collection of microscopic facets with specific normal distributions. It separates the surface geometry (Normal Distribution Function) from the microfacet orientation and [Fresnel reflection](#9067-fresnel-reflection-refraction.md). Suitable for glossy and metallic surfaces. See [Microfacet BRDF](52-microfacet-brdf.md).

### Lobe-based BRDF
Approximates the BRDF as a sum of analytical lobes (e.g., diffuse, specular) with parameters for color and roughness. Efficient for real-time rendering but less physically accurate than microfacet models for complex materials. See [Lobe-based BRDF](52-lobe-brdf.md).

### Measured BRDF
Uses empirical data captured from real materials to define the BRDF. Provides high fidelity for specific objects but lacks generalization and requires large data storage. See [Measured BRDF](52-measured-brdf.md).
